hegde-killer-app-definition: Section 2, p.2: the paper says 'what we call a killer app' and defines it in that sentence. The value matches.
hegde-position-three-strategies: Abstract and Section 1, p.1: the paper calls itself a position paper and lists its three strategies (killer app, AI and quantum, co-design). The stored value matches the passage.
heimann-contributions: Section I, p.2: the four contributions are listed in the authors' own words. The value says only what the authors state they do.
heimann-scope-one-dim-fourier: Section I, p.2: guidelines drawn from numerics on one-dimensional truncated Fourier series; the authors conclude they transfer but say 'this assumption may not hold universally'. The value reports the conclusion as the authors' own and gives the caveat.
heimann-learning-capability-definition: Section III A, p.4, Eq. (7) and (8): mu_d is the average over G_d (random normalized Fourier functions of degree d) of the final validation MSE.
heimann-set-size-100: Section III A, p.4: |G_d| = 100 with the stated reason, and smaller sizes not considered. Appendix H compares set sizes.
heimann-can-gate-definition: Section III B, p.4: CAN(theta) = RXX RYY RZZ, three trainable parameters, tested to bridge to dQNN ansatze. The value matches.
heimann-entanglement-layer-definition: Section III B, p.5, Fig. 2: entanglement layers are blocks of each W, rotations then controlled gates; strong entanglement sets the range equal to the block number.
heimann-dqnn-reupload-design: Section III B, p.6, Fig. 4b and 4c: data encoding on every qubit but the output one; the zero-layer variant adds single-qubit gates before each encoding gate.
heimann-dqnn-training-method: Section III B, p.6: the paper states it does not use the parameter matrix multiplication rule of [29] and uses the layered-ansatz gradient method.
heimann-simulation-setup: Section III C, p.6: TensorFlow Quantum with qsim and Cirq, Adjoint gradients, analytic expectation values in the main text (shot-based in Appendix B).
heimann-training-hyperparameters: Section III C, p.6: Adam, at most 360 epochs, learning rate 0.5, 0.1, 0.05 in blocks of 120 epochs.
heimann-loss-cutoff: Section III C, p.6-7: training stops at loss 5e-5, called quasiperfect (average absolute error 0.7%); the authors note this cutoff corresponds to overfitting.
heimann-significance-marker: Section III C, p.7: gray marker at 6.25e-4 (under 5% absolute error); below it losses are treated as equal in learning capability.
heimann-encoding-measurement-fixed: Section III C, p.7: RX encoding and a sigma-z measurement on the last qubit, for layered PQCs and dQNNs.
heimann-noise-model-use: Section III C, p.6 and Appendix C: a simulated noise model from IBM Falcon r5.11H calibration data, used to show the measure can be determined under noise.
heimann-limit-multivariate-hardware: Section V, p.13: multi-variate functions are an important next step; real hardware and other gradient methods need further research. The authors state what the work does not cover.
heimann-lie-algebra-definition: Appendix A, Definition A.2, p.14: the dynamical Lie algebra is the Lie algebra spanned by repeated nested commutators of the generators G (encoding, parameterized and entangling).
heimann-lemma-a1: Appendix A, Lemma A.1, p.14: stated with its conditions (distinct single-qubit Paulis P_i and O_i on each qubit) and proved in one line from the su(2) relations. The proof is terse but complete: two distinct Paulis generate su(2) on each qubit, and different qubits commute.
heimann-appendixc-noise-sim: Appendix C, p.16: the authors state their two reasons for simulated noise: limited hardware access with millions of circuit evaluations, and transpilation to a native gate set could bias results.
heimann-appendixc-device: Appendix C 1, p.16-17: ibmq perth (Falcon r5.11H), seven qubits, five copied to make 12; Table I caption says calibration data was obtained on June 1st, 2023.
heimann-appendixc-noise-limits: Appendix C 2, p.17-18: 'a more detailed investigation is out of scope'; the set is restricted to 10 low cross-correlation functions and values are normalized below one. The authors state the scope of the noise experiment themselves.
heimann-appendixd-limit: Appendix D, p.19: 'since our grid test could still miss an important hyperparameter set' is the authors' own caveat on their hyperparameter test.
heimann-appendixe-function-generation: Appendix E, p.19-20: each coefficient is a + ib with a and b uniform on [-0.5, 0.5], the -omega coefficient is the complex conjugate, and the series is normalized to maximum absolute value 1.
heimann-example6-spectrum: Appendix K, Example 6, p.31: the paper's own calculation for n qubits and L layers gives the frequency set as the integers from -nL to nL, using the eigenvalue sums of the RX encodings. It restates the spectrum result of Ref. [33] (Appendix F says so) but derives it here.
heimann-example1-c0-zero: Appendix K, Example 1, p.30: a general unitary W, S = RX, Z measurement; the calculation ends with c0 = 0. The conditions are in the preamble of Appendix K 1 (checked: the Bloch-vector argument agrees).
heimann-example2-c0-zero: Appendix K, Example 2, p.30: a general unitary W applied first, then RX, Z measurement; the calculation shows c0 = 0 (the factor 1 - 1). The conditions are in the Appendix K 1 preamble.
heimann-example3-real-coefficients: Appendix K, Example 3, p.30-31: for W = RY all matrix entries are real, so the products in c0 and c1 are real. The statement is limited to W = RY, as the value says.
heimann-limit-transfer-to-general-qml: Section V, p.13: the authors say the Fourier-series-to-general-QML assumption 'may not hold universally' and that all experiments use RX encoding of one-dimensional data. Both are caveats on their own work.
hein-scope-learn-environment: Abstract and Section I, p.1-2: the paper states it learns the environment parameters by QML on hardware (Section III, IBM) and then uses them in QPE on hardware (Section IV, IonQ). The value says only what the authors state they demonstrate.
hein-bandit-definition: Section III, p.2: the paper defines the two-armed bandit in its own words, with one state, two arms and rewards 0 or 1.
hein-closed-form-angles: Section III A, p.3, Eq. (8) and (9): the paper gives the inverted formulas and says it uses them only as reference points because they bypass the noisy-hardware learning goal.
hein-learning-setup: Section III C and D, p.3-4: cost is the MSE between f_meas and f_data, 8000 shots per circuit, COBYLA from scipy.optimize.minimize for two parameter settings (70/20 and 0/50). All three facts are the paper's stated setup.
hein-qpe-policy-values: Section IV B, p.4: 'The true values of these policies are v50 = 0.45 and v0 = 0.2.' They follow from the stated arm probabilities (0.5*0.7+0.5*0.2 and 0.2). Benchmark values of the paper's own setup.
hein-conclusion-noise-limit: Section V, p.5: the authors state that noise and gate errors complicate the application of this QRL approach on current hardware. It is a caveat on their own work, not a measurement.
qpe-setup: Section IV B, p.4-5: IonQ forte-1 (gate-based, trapped ions), n = 3 and 4 with 5 and 6 qubits and 412 and 883 gates, 300 runs per circuit, two policies (50% and 0% left), bandit arms 70% and 20% from Section III. The widened value says only what the paper states about its setup.
hellstern-scope: Abstract, p.1: the paper states it treats feature selection as a QUBO, compares results on small setups and extends to 27 features. The value says only that.
hellstern-qubo-objective: Section 2.2, p.3, Eq. (1)-(3): the paper defines its objective with the inter-feature term, the target term and the weight phi in [0,1], called a hyper-parameter. The value matches.
hellstern-dependency-measures: Section 2.2, p.3: for inter-feature dependence the paper restricts itself to correlation and mutual information; for the target it tested all four measures (correlation, MI, ROC, ANOVA).
hellstern-datasets: Section 3.1, p.3-4: lending club subset (8 features, 1000 observations) and Wisconsin breast cancer (10 features, 569), logistic regression, whole data set used for training.
hellstern-overfitting-caveat: Section 3.1, p.4: the authors state they are aware that training on the whole data set may lead to overfitting. The value attributes the robustness argument to the authors as their argument, so it adds no unproved claim.
hellstern-auroc-criterion: Section 3.1, p.4: the paper states it chose AUROC as the measure to optimize, with the imbalance reason. A choice of its own protocol.
hellstern-qaoa-setup: Section 4.1, p.7: standard mixer, 8192 shots, classical optimizer on the expectation value, and all quantum calculations in IBM Qiskit with out-of-the-box QAOA and VQE. All are stated setup.
hellstern-approx-ratio-definition: Section 4.1, p.7, Eq. (9): r = (h - hmax)/(hmin - hmax), with hmax the worst and hmin the best bit string; the paper says ratio 1 means the optimum with probability 1.
hellstern-vqe-ansatz: Section 4.1, p.7: VQE with the real-amplitudes ansatz: one parametrized RY per qubit and CNOTs between neighbors, repeated for several layers.
hellstern-qaoa-initialization: Section 4.2.1, p.9-10 and Fig. 5: the four initialization heuristics for increasing p, as proposed in [5]. The paper states it uses them. The value says 'as proposed in an earlier study', so no credit is claimed for the method.
hellstern-hardware-not-comparable: Section 4.2.2, p.12: 'We are aware ... results from different machines are not directly comparable' and the next sentence gives the availability reason. A caveat on the paper's own comparison.
hellstern-27-proof-of-concept: Section 5, p.15: the real-device run 'should be considered a proof of concept'. The paper states the choice of IBM's standard untuned QAOA with its two reasons, and the CPLEX optimum as ground truth. Reported as the authors' own stated reasons and setup.
hellstern-27-ratio-definitions: Section 5, p.15: the paper defines the ratio relative to CPLEX (best and worst CPLEX values) and relative to simulation (best and worst simulation values, 'the spread').
hellstern-metaheuristics-tested: Section 5.2 and 5.2.5, p.16-18: EA, SAEA, UEDA, DCMA, plus greedy local search with restarts and random search as baselines.
hellstern-experiment-design: Section 5.3, p.18: random split into two subsets, each generating a QUBO; one for tuning, one for validation; QAOA nine runs at p = 3 on real devices (mainly Geneva and Montreal) on the validation instance only; CPLEX solves it exactly.
hellstern-tuning-procedure: Section 5.3.1, p.18: 100 random configurations per algorithm, 10 runs each, maximum 2000 OFE per run, best median performance chosen.
hellstern-qaoa-untuned: Section 5.3.1, p.19: QAOA is not tuned because system access does not allow the larger run count; the metaheuristics are not specialized to quadratic objectives. Both are caveats the authors state on the fairness of their comparison.
hellstern-discussion-small-demo: Section 6, p.23: the authors say the small-size solutions 'merely served to demonstrate the feasibility' and that the 27-feature problem is more interesting. A statement of what the small runs are for.
hellstern-scaling-open: Section 6, p.23: 'An open question that will be addressed in future work is the scaling of both approaches, i.e. if and for which number of qubits there may be a quantum advantage.' The paper states what it does not settle.
henke-qubo-derivation: Section 2.1, p.3, Eq. (1)-(5): the paper expands the energy, defines h_i = -x^T D_i + D_i^T D_i + lambda and Q_i = D_i^T D, absorbs the self term into the linear term and states the QUBO H(h,Q,a). The value matches the paper's own formulation.
henke-single-image: Section 2.1, p.4: one fashion MNIST image, 28x28 divided into 16 patches of 7x7, 64 variables per patch, plus a 128-variable version (Section 3.1: four QUBOs).
henke-dictionary-learning-sa: Section 2.1, p.3: the QUBOs use the un-normalized dictionary learning of [26], performed with simulated annealing.
henke-loihi2-nebm-params: Section 2.3.6, p.6: linear schedule, Tmax 15, 20 steps per temperature, 6000 time steps, sampled every 20 steps, 300 samples per run.
henke-iterated-warm-start-definition: Section 2.3.6, p.6: the paper defines iterated warm starting: standard run from a random binary vector, best solution initializes the next run, repeated 100 times.
henke-dwave-device: Section 2.4 and 2.4.1, p.7: Advantage system4.1, Pegasus graph, 5627 programmable qubits and 40279 couplers, all results on this device.
henke-parallel-embeddings: Section 2.4.1, p.7-8 and Fig. 7: parallel quantum annealing, seven disjoint 64-variable embeddings and two disjoint 128-variable embeddings, all-to-all.
henke-reverse-anneal-schedule: Section 2.4.2, p.8: schedule {[0,1],[10,s],[90,s],[100,1]} for all reverse annealing experiments, with s varied.
henke-qemc-definition: Section 2.4.3, p.8-9: the paper defines its QEMC: chained reverse anneals, each initialized with the best solution of the last set, start from a 100 microsecond forward anneal with 1000 samples, batch of anneals at each step.
henke-sa-setup: Section 2.5, p.9: dwave-neal, 1000 reads per QUBO, other settings default, geometric schedule.
henke-cplex-setup: Section 2.6, p.9: CPLEX solves each QUBO exactly with no time limit; it does not report whether optima are degenerate and the authors leave ground-state degeneracy to future research.
henke-fig3-conditions: Figure 3 caption, p.10: reconstructions are the best mean energy and sparsity across the 16 QUBOs for the best parameter set per technique; the forward anneal used no parallel QA and 20 microseconds.
henke-table1-sample-sources: Section 3, p.11: Loihi 1 minima from 2000 samples across device parameters (from [26]); Loihi 2 minima from the 100 samples of iterated warm starting.
henke-degeneracy-limit: Section 3, p.12: 'as CPLEX only returns one optimal solution, the reported CPLEX results do not capture the case of more than one optimal solution with different sparsity.'
henke-future-scaling: Section 4, p.14: the authors name scaling with future processors against classical algorithms, and larger sparse coding QUBOs, as open for future work.
henke-benchmarks: Abstract, p.1, with Section 2.5 and 2.6 and Table 1: simulated annealing is the benchmark and CPLEX computes the optimal energies. The paper states its own protocol.

theory_low.heimann-lemma-a2: Appendix A, Lemma A.2, p.15: the lemma does not state what U in G_ent = {U_{i+1} - Z_i U_{i+1}} is. For U = identity the claim fails. The 'proof' is one sketched commutator step. The conditions are lost and the proof is informal.
theory_low.heimann-proposition-a4: Appendix A, Proposition A.4, p.15: the proof says 'a similar argument can be made' and 'Clearly' for the step to n-body terms. It is an informal sketch built on Lemma A.2, whose conditions are incomplete.
theory_low.heimann-corollary-a5: Appendix A, Corollary A.5, p.15: it rests on Proposition A.4 (a sketch). It also applies A.4 to 'any circuit' of the paper without checking the cyclic, CAN and dQNN circuits. The barren plateau conclusion uses the result of Ref. [52] (full-rank DLA), which is cited, not proved here.
